questions.stem: An energy level diagram shows reactants at 200 kJ and products at 50 kJ. What is the enthalpy change (Delta H) for this reaction?

options.text: -50 kJ

questions.explanation: Delta H = energy of products - energy of reactants = 50 - 200 = -150 kJ. The negative sign indicates this is an exothermic reaction - the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants, so energy has been released to the surroundings.

questions.stem: A reaction profile shows the reactants at a lower level than the products, with a large peak between them. Which features can be identified from this diagram?

options.text: The reaction is exothermic with a high activation energy
The reaction is endothermic with a high activation energy
The reaction is endothermic with no activation energy
The reaction is exothermic with no activation energy

questions.explanation: Products at a higher level than reactants means the reaction is endothermic (energy is absorbed). The large peak represents the activation energy - the minimum energy needed for the reaction to occur. All reactions have activation energy; the peak between reactants and products always represents this energy barrier.

questions.stem: On an energy level diagram, the activation energy for a reaction is 80 kJ and the overall enthalpy change is -120 kJ. What is the energy of the products relative to the peak of the energy barrier?

options.text: 40 kJ below the peak
120 kJ below the peak
200 kJ below the peak
80 kJ below the peak

questions.explanation: The peak is 80 kJ above the reactants (activation energy). The products are 120 kJ below the reactants (Delta H = -120 kJ). So the products are 80 + 120 = 200 kJ below the peak. The activation energy for the reverse reaction would be 200 kJ.

questions.stem: Two reactions have the same enthalpy change of -50 kJ. Reaction A has an activation energy of 30 kJ and Reaction B has an activation energy of 150 kJ. Which reaction would proceed faster at room temperature?

options.text: Reaction B, because it has more energy to release
Both proceed at the same rate because they have the same enthalpy change
Reaction A, because fewer particles need to overcome the lower energy barrier
Neither would proceed because both are exothermic

questions.explanation: The rate of reaction depends on activation energy, not enthalpy change. Reaction A has a lower activation energy (30 kJ), meaning more particles at room temperature have enough energy to react upon collision. Reaction B requires much more energy (150 kJ) for successful collisions, so fewer particles can react and the rate is slower.

questions.stem: A student draws an energy level diagram for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2). The diagram shows products lower than reactants. She adds a catalyst (manganese dioxide) to the reaction. How would the energy level diagram change?

options.text: The products would be at an even lower energy level
The activation energy peak would be lower, but reactant and product energy levels stay the same
Both the activation energy and enthalpy change would decrease
The reactants would be at a higher energy level

questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. It does NOT change the energy levels of reactants or products, so the enthalpy change (Delta H) remains the same. On the diagram, only the height of the energy barrier (peak) decreases. The catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the overall energy change.
